blocks.content: ETHAN

Mr. Alvarez had my coffee on the counter before the door finished closing behind me. I've been coming here long enough that I think of us as friends. He probably thinks of me as a reliable revenue stream. I've decided these aren't mutually exclusive.

blocks.speaker: Mr. Alvarez
blocks.content: You are late.

blocks.speaker: Ethan
blocks.content: You opened three minutes ago.

blocks.speaker: Mr. Alvarez
blocks.content: Late.
I paid. He gave me the coffee. This is our entire relationship and I find it deeply satisfying.
Corner table. Sketchbook open. Pencil tapped twice against a blank page.
Blank pages don't scare me. People do. These are related facts.

The town was waking up outside the window. Delivery truck. Woman with flowers. Two kids outside the bakery in a serious dispute over pastry allocation. I started drawing without thinking too hard — curb, bookstore sign, bakery awning, people as movement before detail. That's usually when the good stuff happens.
Then I saw her.

Across the street, walking with another girl, both of them laughing, both carrying drinks. She had a purple stuffed dinosaur tucked under one arm like it was nothing. Like she won things from rigged machines every day.
My pencil stopped.
I looked down at my page.

I had drawn her into the street scene. Not her face — just movement. The tilt of her shoulders. The loose fall of her hair. The dinosaur, which I had apparently rendered with enough anatomical detail to suggest I had been watching significantly longer than I thought.
I flipped the page before Mr. Alvarez could see.
He had absolutely already seen.

blocks.speaker: Mr. Alvarez
blocks.content: Two sugars. Because bitterness should only exist in art.

blocks.speaker: Ethan
blocks.content: You say that every time.

blocks.speaker: Mr. Alvarez
blocks.content: It is true every time.
I became very interested in my coffee.
